**My reasoning as this farmer:**

I've been farming this land for over 30 years, and I know Quzhou well. The North China Plain gives us cold, dry winters and hot, rainy summers — the wheat-maize rotation is the backbone of everything here, and I see no reason to change what works. I farm about 25 mu, including 8 mu I rent from neighbors who moved to the city. My sons are in Handan, so I run this mostly alone now.

I'll grow winter wheat into summer, then flip to maize on the same ground — same as always. I won't chase cotton or vegetables; at my age and with limited labor, simplicity matters. I know exactly what these fields need.

For wheat, I'll use 石农086 — a certified improved variety bred for Hebei conditions, good disease resistance, stable yield. Not traditional seed, not expensive hybrid, just solid improved seed. I'll do rotary tillage after maize harvest to break up the stubble properly, then apply base fertilizer before seeding. I'll top-dress nitrogen at jointing. I'll irrigate three times: the winter freeze-protection water in November, jointing water in April, and grain-fill water in May. Three pesticide runs: fall herbicide, spring herbicide plus foliar fungicide, then a combined fungicide-insecticide spray at heading to guard against rust and aphids.

For maize, I direct-seed into wheat stubble — no-tillage saves me labor and fuel. Hybrid seed, 郑单958 is what I've trusted for years. Summer rain covers most water needs; I'll only irrigate at planting if it's dry, and again around tasseling if rainfall is short. Two pesticide passes: early herbicide, then corn borer control mid-season.

I'm aware of the groundwater situation in Quzhou — the county has been pushing water quotas. Three wheat irrigations is already conservative compared to what older farmers do, and I'll use my ground-pipe system to reduce losses.
